```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
okabe_ito <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7")
```

Nine exercises for courses on visual communication, information design,
data visualisation, accessibility and research methods. Each has a question
for students, a hint, and a worked solution. Because the data are synthetic,
the "right answer" is known: compare your results with
`metadata/true_effects.csv`.

> **Remind students that the data are synthetic.** Results describe the
> simulation model, not real audiences.

This notebook lives in `examples/` and reads the files relative to it.
Render it with `rmarkdown::render("examples/teaching-exercises.Rmd")`, or
run the chunks one by one with the working directory set to `examples/`.
It needs only base R (and the rmarkdown package to render).

```{r load}
designs <- read.csv("../data/synthetic_designs.csv", na.strings = "")
participants <- read.csv("../data/synthetic_participants.csv")
responses <- read.csv("../data/synthetic_responses.csv")
true_effects <- read.csv("../metadata/true_effects.csv")
source("../code/generator.R")  # only needed for exercise 8
```

Most exercises start from the joined table:

```{r}
study <- merge(merge(responses, designs, by = "design_id"),
               participants, by = "participant_id")
```

## 1. Describe the corpus

**Question.** What kinds of artefacts are in `designs`? How do word count
and imagery differ between them?

*Hint:* `table()`, `tapply()` and `boxplot()` are enough.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```{r}
table(designs$artefact_type)
round(tapply(designs$word_count, designs$artefact_type, median))
boxplot(image_text_ratio ~ artefact_type, data = designs, col = "#56B4E9",
        border = "grey30", xlab = "", ylab = "Share of area that is imagery")
```

Infographics are the wordiest, social media images the most image-heavy and
data charts the least.
</details>

## 2. Accessibility audit

**Question.** What share of designs fails WCAG 2 AA text contrast? Does it
vary by artefact type? Which of the failing designs have no text
alternative?

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```{r}
round(100 * (1 - mean(designs$wcag_aa_contrast)), 1)
round(100 * tapply(!designs$wcag_aa_contrast, designs$artefact_type, mean), 1)
with(designs, table(fails_aa = !wcag_aa_contrast, alt_text))
```

Slides fail least often, because large text only needs 3:1.
</details>

## 3. Who is excluded by low contrast?

**Question.** Compare comprehension for participants with typical colour
vision and with red-green colour vision deficiency (deutan or protan), for
designs with complementary or triadic palettes, below and above 4.5:1.

*Hint:* the effect is an interaction. Plot it.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```{r cvd}
sub <- study[study$colour_harmony %in% c("complementary", "triadic") & !study$low_vision, ]
sub$vision <- ifelse(sub$colour_vision %in% c("deutan", "protan"), "red-green CVD", "typical")
sub$aa <- ifelse(sub$contrast_ratio >= 4.5, "4.5:1 or more", "below 4.5:1")
m <- with(sub, tapply(comprehension_score, list(vision, aa), mean))
round(m, 2)
barplot(m, beside = TRUE, col = okabe_ito[c(1, 4)], border = NA, ylim = c(0, 5),
        legend.text = TRUE, args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bty = "n"),
        ylab = "Mean correct answers (of 5)")
```

Above 4.5:1 the two groups are close; below it the gap widens because
colour vision deficiency lowers the contrast experienced. Discuss why the
sample of participants with colour vision deficiency is small, and what
that means for the precision of the estimate.
</details>

## 4. Choose the right chart

**Question.** Show how comprehension changes with contrast ratio. Which
scale should the x axis use, and why?

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```{r scale}
bins <- cut(study$contrast_ratio, breaks = exp(seq(log(1.2), log(21), length.out = 15)),
            include.lowest = TRUE)
mid <- tapply(study$contrast_ratio, bins, median)
y <- tapply(study$comprehension_score, bins, mean)
plot(mid, y, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#0072B2", ylim = c(0, 5),
     xlab = "Contrast ratio (log scale)", ylab = "Mean correct answers (of 5)")
abline(v = 4.5, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
text(4.5, 0.4, "WCAG AA", pos = 4, col = "grey30")
```

Contrast ratios are multiplicative (from 1:1 to 21:1), so a log axis spreads
the values evenly. The curve rises steeply up to 4.5:1 and flattens after.
</details>

## 5. Model comprehension

**Question.** Fit a logistic regression for the number of correct answers
(out of five) with contrast below and above 4.5:1, focal point, word count
and visual literacy. Compare the coefficients with the true effects.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```{r}
study$lc <- log(study$contrast_ratio / 4.5)
fit <- glm(cbind(comprehension_score, 5 - comprehension_score) ~
             pmin(lc, 0) + pmax(lc, 0) + focal_point + log(word_count / 50) +
             I(visual_literacy - 50),
           family = binomial, data = study)
round(coef(fit), 3)
eff <- true_effects
eff[eff$outcome == "comprehension" &
      eff$term %in% c("log_contrast_below_aa", "log_contrast_above_aa", "focal_point",
                      "log_word_count", "visual_literacy"), c("term", "value")]
```

Contrast, focal point and visual literacy are close to the truth. The
word count effect is too strong: wordier designs are also more complex
(`visual_complexity` is computed partly from word count), and complexity
lowers comprehension too. Leaving it out of the model loads its effect onto
word count, which is omitted-variable bias. Add `I(visual_complexity - 50)`
and the word count estimate falls to about -0.30.

The remaining estimates are slightly smaller than the true values for two
reasons. The model ignores the random effects for designs and participants,
which pulls population-average log-odds towards zero (`lme4::glmer()` with
`(1 | design_id) + (1 | participant_id)` gets closer). It also uses the
nominal contrast ratio rather than the effective one.
</details>

## 6. Aesthetic judgement and expertise

**Question.** Does alignment consistency matter more to professional
designers than to other participants?

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```{r}
fit <- lm(aesthetic_rating ~ alignment_consistency * design_expertise, data = study)
round(coef(summary(fit))[, 1:2], 3)
```

The interaction term for professionals is clearly positive. Discuss the
choice of treating a 1-7 rating as numeric, and try `MASS::polr()` for an
ordinal model.
</details>

## 7. Direct and indirect paths to recall

**Question.** Recall depends on comprehension and dwell time. Does the
estimated effect of a human face, and of visual complexity, change when you
control for them?

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```{r}
study$cx <- study$visual_complexity - 50
paths <- function(term) {
  total <- glm(reformulate(term, "recall_24h"), family = binomial, data = study)
  direct <- glm(reformulate(c(term, "comprehension_score", "log(dwell_time_s)"), "recall_24h"),
                family = binomial, data = study)
  c(total = coef(total)[[2]], direct = coef(direct)[[2]])
}
round(rbind(human_face = paths("human_face"), complexity_per_point = paths("cx")), 4)
```

Faces act on recall only directly in the generating model
(`r true_effects$value[true_effects$outcome == "recall_24h" & true_effects$term == "human_face"]`
on the logit scale), so both estimates are about the same. Complexity
also has indirect paths: it lowers comprehension (less recall) and lengthens
dwell time (more recall). Controlling for the mediators moves its estimate
towards the direct effect of -0.010. Discuss which estimate answers which
question, and why controlling for a mediator is not always what you want.
</details>

## 8. How many participants do you need?

**Question.** A class study can recruit 30 participants who each see 10
designs. How often would such a study detect the effect of a focal point on
comprehension at the 5% level?

*Hint:* use `vc_generate()` from `code/generator.R` with different seeds.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```{r power}
detect <- vapply(1:40, function(s) {
  sim <- vc_generate(n_designs = 200, n_participants = 30,
                     trials_per_participant = 10, seed = 1000 + s)
  d <- merge(sim$responses, sim$designs, by = "design_id")
  fit <- glm(cbind(comprehension_score, 5 - comprehension_score) ~ focal_point,
             family = binomial, data = d)
  coef(summary(fit))["focal_pointTRUE", 4] < 0.05
}, logical(1))
mean(detect)
```

Repeat with 60 or 120 participants and plot the detection rate. This is a
simulation-based power analysis; the same approach works for any planned
design study, as long as students are clear that the effect sizes are
assumptions.
</details>

## 9. Critique the images

**Question.** Every design has an image in `images/`. Find the three
designs with the lowest and the three with the highest mean comprehension.
Look at their images: which visible features would you blame, and does the
table agree?

*Hint:* `metadata/images.csv` gives each design's file and the contrast
actually drawn.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```{r images}
images <- read.csv("../metadata/images.csv")
score <- tapply(responses$comprehension_score, responses$design_id, mean)
ids <- names(sort(score))[c(1:3, (length(score) - 2):length(score))]
cols <- c("design_id", "artefact_type", "contrast_ratio", "word_count",
          "hierarchy_levels", "visual_complexity", "focal_point")
cbind(designs[match(ids, designs$design_id), cols], mean_score = round(score[ids], 2))
```

```{r image-grid, echo = FALSE, out.width = "32%", fig.show = "hold"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path("..", images$image_file[match(ids, images$design_id)]))
```

The weakest designs usually combine low contrast with many words or high
complexity; the strongest have high contrast, a focal point and short text.
Mean scores rest on only about ten responses per design, so chance also
plays a part. A good follow-up: pick two images that look similar but score
differently, and explain the difference from the table.
</details>

## For discussion

- What would you need to change in this model to make it more realistic?
- Why must a synthetic result never be reported as a finding about people?
- Which real study could you design to test one of these effects, and what
  ethical approvals would it need?
